subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which instrument is used to measure wind speed?
questions.explain: An anemometer, usually with rotating cups, records wind speed, often in km/h or knots.

questions.q: A rain gauge measures precipitation. In which unit is the reading normally recorded?
questions.explain: Rainfall collected in a rain gauge is measured as a depth of water in millimetres.

questions.q: Which instrument measures atmospheric (air) pressure?
questions.explain: A barometer measures atmospheric pressure, typically in millibars (mb).

questions.q: Why is a Stevenson screen painted white and fitted with louvred (slatted) sides?
options: To reflect heat and allow air to circulate freely around the instruments
To absorb as much sunlight as possible to warm the thermometers
To keep the instruments completely sealed from all outside air
To make the box heavy so it does not blow away in strong winds
questions.explain: White paint reflects solar radiation and the louvres let air flow through, so instruments record true shaded air conditions.

questions.q: A synoptic chart shows an area of low pressure moving towards the UK. What weather is most likely?
options: Cloud, rain and unsettled conditions as air rises
Clear skies and dry, settled conditions as air sinks
Persistent fog with no wind for several days
A long spell of frost and high pressure
questions.explain: In low pressure (a depression) air rises, cools and condenses, producing cloud and rain.

questions.q: On a weather map, what do isobars represent?
options: Lines joining places of equal atmospheric pressure
Lines joining places of equal temperature
Lines joining places of equal rainfall
questions.explain: Isobars connect points of equal air pressure, measured in millibars.

questions.q: On a synoptic chart, what does it indicate when isobars are very close together?
questions.explain: Closely spaced isobars show a steep pressure gradient, which produces stronger winds.

questions.q: Moist air from the sea is forced to rise over a coastal mountain range, cools and produces rain on the windward slope. Which type of rainfall is this?
questions.explain: Relief rainfall occurs when air is forced to rise over high ground, cooling and condensing.

questions.q: How is the general climate of the UK best described?
questions.explain: The UK has a cool temperate maritime climate: mild, wet and without extremes due to oceanic influence.

questions.q: Which greenhouse gas is released in the greatest quantity by the burning of fossil fuels?
questions.explain: Burning fossil fuels such as coal, oil and gas releases large amounts of carbon dioxide, the main human-caused greenhouse gas.

questions.q: What is meant by the 'enhanced greenhouse effect'?
options: Extra greenhouse gases trapping more heat and warming the atmosphere
The natural cooling of the planet by cloud cover
The blocking of all incoming solar radiation by pollution
A reduction in greenhouse gases causing global cooling
questions.explain: Human activity adds greenhouse gases that trap additional outgoing heat, strengthening the natural greenhouse effect and warming the planet.

questions.q: Which of the following provides evidence of past climate and atmospheric CO2 over thousands of years?
questions.explain: Trapped air bubbles in ice cores reveal past temperatures and CO2 concentrations going back thousands of years.

questions.q: Which of the following is a NATURAL cause of climate change?
options: Major volcanic eruptions and variations in the Sun's output
questions.explain: Volcanic activity, changes in solar output and Milankovitch cycles are natural causes, whereas the others are human causes.

questions.q: A low-lying coastal community is worried about flooding of homes over the coming decades. Which effect of climate change is the most direct cause of this concern?
questions.explain: Melting ice and thermal expansion of warming oceans raise sea levels, increasing flood risk for low-lying coasts.

questions.q: Tropical storms generally only form over oceans where the surface water temperature is at least about:
questions.explain: Sea surface temperatures of roughly 26.5-27°C or above provide the heat and moisture needed for tropical storms to develop.

questions.q: Why is the eye at the centre of a tropical storm calm, with clear skies?
options: Air is sinking (descending) in the eye
Air is rising rapidly in the eye
The eye is over cold ocean water
Rain is heaviest in the eye
questions.explain: In the eye air descends, which suppresses cloud formation and creates calm, clear conditions.

questions.q: What does the Saffir-Simpson scale measure?
options: The intensity of a tropical storm, based mainly on wind speed
The amount of rainfall in a thunderstorm
The height of storm surge waves only
The air pressure at the centre of a depression
questions.explain: The Saffir-Simpson scale classifies tropical storms into categories 1-5 according to sustained wind speed.

questions.q: A geographer notes that tropical storms do not form right on the Equator, even though the sea there is very warm. What best explains this?
options: There is no Coriolis effect at the Equator to make the storm spin
The sea at the Equator is too cold
There is too little moisture at the Equator
Air pressure at the Equator is always very high
questions.explain: The Coriolis effect, needed to spin a storm, is zero at the Equator, so storms form a few degrees to the north or south.

questions.q: Winds are named according to the direction they blow FROM. A wind blowing from the west towards the east is therefore called a:
questions.explain: Winds are named by their source direction, so a wind coming from the west is a westerly.

questions.q: Convectional rainfall is most likely to occur:
options: On a hot afternoon when the ground heats air that rises rapidly
When air is forced up and over a mountain range
When a warm air mass meets a cold air mass at a front
During a long spell of high pressure and clear skies
questions.explain: Intense surface heating makes air rise quickly, cooling and condensing into towering clouds and heavy showers.
